theory.intro: The mean uses **every** value, so a long tail drags it towards that tail. The median only counts **positions** in the ordered data, and the mode sits at the peak. That difference lets you read the order of the measures from the shape.
facts: To the median one very large value counts as just one value, no matter how large it is.
The **mode** never moves off the peak and the **mean** always finishes nearest the tail, with the median between them.
It also works in reverse: a mean well **above** the median means the tail is on the right.
A mean well **below** the median means the tail is on the left.
A **uniform** distribution is symmetrical, so its mean and median are equal.
Every value in a uniform distribution occurs equally often, so it has **no mode** to compare with them.
steps: Name the skew from the tail
Place the mode at the peak
Order the measures with the mean nearest the tail

foundation.question_text:
At a walk-in clinic the waiting times have a mean of $24$ minutes, a median of $18$ minutes and a mode of $15$ minutes.
Describe the shape of the distribution of the waiting times.
foundation.solution_text:
$\text{mode} = 15$, $\text{median} = 18$ and $\text{mean} = 24$, so $\text{mode} < \text{median} < \text{mean}$.
The mean is the largest of the three, so it has been dragged away from the peak towards a tail on the right.
Positively skewed.

foundation.question_text:
The times taken by a class to finish a timed quiz have a mean of $9.4$ minutes, a median of $10$ minutes and a mode of $11$ minutes.
Describe the shape of the distribution of the times.
foundation.solution_text:
$\text{mean} = 9.4$, $\text{median} = 10$ and $\text{mode} = 11$, so $\text{mean} < \text{median} < \text{mode}$.
The mean is the smallest of the three, so it has been dragged away from the peak towards a tail on the left.
Negatively skewed.

foundation.question_text:
A testing app records a large set of reaction times.
The mean is $302$ milliseconds, the median is $301$ milliseconds and the mode is $300$ milliseconds.
Describe the shape of the distribution of the reaction times.
foundation.solution_text:
The three measures differ by at most $2$ milliseconds in times of about $300$ milliseconds, so $\text{mean} \approx \text{median} \approx \text{mode}$.
No tail has dragged the mean away from the peak.
Symmetrical.

The mode is the most common waiting time, so it must lie in the tallest column, the $0\text{--}10$ class.
Only one of the three lines lies in that class; $Q$ and $R$ lie further to the right, out in the tail, where the median and the mean sit.
The leftmost line, $P$.

foundation.question_text:
In a fun run most runners finish in a similar time, but a few walkers take far longer, so the finishing times are positively skewed.
Explain why the mean finishing time is greater than the median finishing time.
foundation.solution_text:
The mean is found by sharing the total of every finishing time equally, so each very long walking time adds a large amount to that total and pulls the mean up.
The median is only the middle time of the ordered list, so a very long time counts as one time no matter how large it is and barely moves the median.
The long right-hand tail therefore drags the mean above the median.

foundation.question_text:
The times taken to complete a jigsaw puzzle are positively skewed.
The mean, the median and the mode of the times are $26$, $31$ and $40$ minutes, in some order.
Which of these values is the mode?
foundation.solution_text:
For a positively skewed distribution, $\text{mode} < \text{median} < \text{mean}$.
The mode is therefore the smallest of the three values.
$26$ minutes.

development.question_text:

development.solution_text:
The mean is $7$ minutes above the median, so a tail on the right has dragged the mean up.
A tail on the right means the distribution is positively skewed, so $\text{mode} < \text{median} < \text{mean}$.
The mode is therefore below the median, at less than $248$ minutes.

The peak is near the right and the curve trails away over a long stretch to the left, so the distribution is negatively skewed and $\text{mean} < \text{median} < \text{mode}$.

development.question_text:
The times a class used to finish a timed quiz are negatively skewed.
Explain why the mean is the smallest of the three measures of centre and the mode is the largest.
development.solution_text:
A negatively skewed distribution has its tail on the left, so a few students finished a long way faster than everybody else.
The mean shares the total of every time equally, so those few very short times pull it down further than any other measure moves.
The median only reports the middle time, so it barely moves, and the mode stays at the peak with the bulk of the class on the right.
That is why $\text{mean} < \text{median} < \text{mode}$.

mastery.question_text:
A report on a medical centre gives the waiting times as mean $= 12$ minutes, median $= 19$ minutes and mode $= 25$ minutes, and describes the distribution as positively skewed.
Explain why the description cannot be correct, and give the correct description.
mastery.solution_text:
The reported values give $\text{mean} < \text{median} < \text{mode}$.
A positively skewed distribution has its tail on the right, which drags the mean above the other two measures, so its mean would have to be the largest of the three.
Here the mean is the smallest, so the tail must stretch to the left instead.
The distribution is negatively skewed.

mastery.question_text:
The finishing times of a marathon are positively skewed.
The three measures of centre are $232$, $246$ and $259$ minutes, in some order.
State which measure each value is, and explain why the largest of the three is the one that the slowest runners affect most.
mastery.solution_text:
For a positively skewed distribution, $\text{mode} < \text{median} < \text{mean}$.
The mode is $232$ minutes, the median is $246$ minutes and the mean is $259$ minutes.
The mean is the largest because it is calculated from the total of every finishing time, so each very slow runner adds a large amount to that total and pulls the mean up towards the tail.
The median only counts positions in the ordered list and the mode stays at the peak, so neither of them is moved much by the slowest runners.

Every column has the same height, so the display is flat, its two halves are mirror images and there is no tail to drag the mean away from the median.
$\overline{x} = \frac{6(6 + 7 + 8 + 9 + 10 + 11)}{36}$
$= \frac{306}{36}$
$= 8.5$
The $18$th time is $8$ minutes and the $19$th is $9$ minutes, so the median is $8.5$ minutes as well.
Every time occurs equally often, so this distribution has no mode at all.
It is not correct: the mean and the median are equal at $8.5$ minutes, but there is no mode to compare them with.
